newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Analysts query Yugoslav inflation forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Analysts query Yugoslav inflation forecasts.

text.p: Independent economists on Friday questioned government forecasts that Yugoslavia's 1996 inflation would fall to a 10-year low of between 50 to 60 per cent.
"Personally, I see the government statistics office forecast a bit optimistic," said Slobodan Milosavljevic, head of the Belgrade-based Market Research Institute (IZIT).
"My opinion is that the price of electricity will have a major effect on retail price growth in November and December."
Milosavljevic and other independent analysts said 1996 inflation would be at least 60 percent or higher.
The federal statistics office said October month-on-month inflation was 1.4 percent and predicted annual inflation would range between 50 and 60 percent compared with 120 percent in 1995.

"Present market conditions do not allow prices to rise," Milosavljevic said. "But reintroduction of the electricity consumption quota will certainly have an ill effect on retail prices in November and December."
According to IZIT's latest report, most Yugoslav firms polled said they expected moderate price growth in the last quarter and only 17 percent of them announced price increases.

"But high inflationary expectations amongst Yugoslav companies in the next six months are worrying," Milosavljevic said. As many as 52 percent of those polled expected to increase their prices in the next six months, he said.
"This means inflation is hidden and that we might have price hikes in the first quarter of next year."
Zoran Popov, an economist of the Economics Institute in Belgrade, disagreed and said "price cuts and not increases are what is needed."
He said the prices of most goods were already 20 to 30 percent above those elsewhere in the world.
Popov predicted inflation would certainly be above 60 percent and said the forecast of 50 to 60 percent was over-optimistic.
"Despite a cumulative 10-month inflation of 49.2 percent on December 1995, annual inflation under 60 percent is not realistic."

Another analyst, who asked not to be named, said federal and local elections due on Sunday "must have influenced the low October retail price index and such a good forecast". --Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom, +38111-222-4254
